item.title: Justices Seem Likely to Side With Colorado Catholic Schools Seeking Public Money
item.description:
The hallways of the St. Mary Catholic Parish school are decorated with Adam-and-Eve-themed apple prints and a colorful mural depicting Jesus’ life as a child. Inside the preschool classroom is a prayer table with a rosary and puzzle pieces shaped like the symbols of Catholicism.

Parents who send their 4-year-olds to the school a few miles south of Denver feel strongly about educating their children in the Catholic faith — but they also say the state of Colorado should pay for it.

And that has led to a clash that reached the Supreme Court on Tuesday. The conservative-dominated bench has issued a series of recent decisions expanding the role of religion in public life, a signature project of the court led by Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr.

After more than two hours of oral argument on Tuesday, the majority seemed likely to continue that trend, with several conservative justices asking skeptical questions of Colorado — and the three liberal justices appearing to side with the state.

At issue is a Colorado program that allows private preschools to get taxpayer funding, but those preschools are required to provide children an “equal opportunity” to enroll, including the children of gay and transgender parents. The Archdiocese of Denver argues that the requirement is at odds with its religious mission — and its members’ First Amendment rights.

The archdiocese, parish and parents sued Colorado, setting up the latest battle at the Supreme Court testing whether religious objections can override government prohibitions against discrimination.

Religious groups almost always prevail before the current Supreme Court. In 2021, the court ruled unanimously that a Catholic social services agency in Philadelphia could defy city rules and refuse to work with same-sex couples who apply to take in foster children. The next year, in a case from Maine, the court said that states that choose to subsidize private schools may not exclude or discriminate against religious ones.

In the Colorado case, however, lower courts have said the state “welcomed and actively solicited” the participation of faith-based preschools after voters approved a universal prekindergarten program in 2020. The state pays for at least 15 hours of free preschool each week at any public or private preschool, including religious ones, provided it meets the program’s requirements, including the nondiscrimination agreement.

In 2023, the archdiocese directed its preschools not to register, arguing the requirements ran counter to its views on sexuality and gender identity. Teachers, other staff members and parents at its schools sign a “statement of community beliefs” that acknowledges that the archdiocese does not recognize same-sex relationships or transgender status. Enrolling children of gay and transgender parents, according to school officials, would “likely lead to intractable conflicts.”

Justice Amy Coney Barrett, who is often in the majority, and Justice Neil M. Gorsuch suggested on Tuesday that even if Colorado’s program was technically open to Catholic schools, the state should have anticipated that the nondiscrimination requirement would preclude their participation.

What is the difference, Justice Barrett asked, between setting up a program that overtly excluded religious schools and “choosing to impose a condition that you know” certain Catholic schools “will be unable to agree to?”

Justice Brett M. Kavanaugh, who is also often a critical vote, asked what harm it would be to grant an exemption to the Catholic schools when plenty of other schools would accept families with gay and transgender parents.

Why not “avoid the clash,” he asked.

In response, Helen Norton, the state’s lawyer, said Colorado had an interest in “ensuring that its public funds go to schools that ensure equal opportunity.” She added that “families are harmed when they’re turned away” from publicly funded schools they choose.

According to the lawsuit, Colorado is excluding hundreds of families across 34 preschools overseen by the archdiocese. As a result, the archbishop of Denver said last week that enrollment is down 20 percent and two preschools have closed, as parents have withdrawn their children and enrolled them in schools that get public funding.

One couple who joined the suit, Dan and Lisa Sheley, met as students at a Catholic college and say they now want their seven children to be steeped in their faith and values both at home and at school, where Lisa works. Because of the state’s policy, the Sheleys said, they have missed out so far on at least $18,000 in tuition assistance. They expect to lose thousands more when another child becomes eligible for the program.

In an interview, Lisa Sheley said the couple voted for the program believing it would be universal. Now, she said, they’ve discovered “it is not universal because we’re being discriminated against and not allowed to participate.”

The school is being represented by lawyers from the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, a religious legal organization. They told the justices in court filings that the government cannot condition access to a public benefit on a recipient’s abandoning their religious beliefs.

“Catholic schools wanted to be a part of it, and Colorado wanted them to be a part of it, but when push came to shove, we couldn’t compromise what we believe,” said Nick Reaves, the lawyer representing the school, parents and archdiocese before the court on Tuesday.

Jared Polis, Colorado’s Democratic governor, said in a statement that state officials intentionally included faith-based groups when they created the program. At least 79 faith-based providers participated in the last school year, serving at least 2,052 students and receiving more than $9.5 million in payments.

In court filings, Colorado’s lawyers argued that the anti-discrimination requirements do not infringe on the schools’ religious beliefs because those schools are free to teach whatever they would like about sex, marriage, gender and family. They need only refrain from excluding children from enrolling “simply because their parents are gay.”

The state also noted that the requirements apply equally to all participating preschools — public, private, secular and religious.

All three liberal justices seemed to embrace the state’s claims and said the Catholic schools were seeking to be treated differently or better than other participating programs and in a way that would discriminate against families with gay and transgender parents.

“Your schools want to discriminate by exclusion,” said Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson. “Nobody else is allowed to do that.”

Both Justices Jackson and Sonia Sotomayor asked why the same line of reasoning would not allow schools to turn away children based on race or ethnicity because of a religious belief.

Scott Skinner-Thompson, a law professor at the University of Colorado who specializes in civil rights and constitutional law, said states have long had the power to impose conditions on recipients of taxpayer funds, such as committing to comply with nondiscrimination requirements.

“St. Mary’s is saying that’s not tenable with our faith position. That’s fine. It’s a simple choice not to take the money,” he said. “The state is trying to balance protecting L.G.B.T.Q. families and preserving religious liberty.”

After a three-day trial, a federal judge said in 2024 that while states may not decline to fund religious schools, states “are not obligated to subsidize discrimination using taxpayer dollars, even when that discrimination is based on religious beliefs.”

A unanimous panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld that decision last year, citing an important Supreme Court precedent limiting First Amendment protections for religious practices.

The 1990 decision, Employment Division v. Smith, said laws that apply neutrally and across the board, without singling out religion, typically do not violate the First Amendment’s protection of the free exercise of religion.

That decision is unpopular among many conservative Christians, who say it does not offer adequate protection to religion. Three justices — Clarence Thomas, Samuel A. Alito Jr. and Justice Gorsuch — have called for overturning that precedent, with Justice Alito writing in 2021 that it “threatens a fundamental freedom.”

Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett expressed hesitation in the same case about the implications of overruling the Smith decision and what would replace it. The court did not directly address the question of whether to overturn it in Tuesday’s argument.

In the court’s 2021 decision in the foster care case from Philadelphia, Chief Justice Roberts said the city’s policies had not met the requirement set out in Smith that laws must be “neutral and generally applicable” because city officials were permitted to make certain exceptions.

Lawyers for the Catholic school in Colorado, backed by the Trump administration, relied on that line of reasoning and asserted that the state has granted exceptions to its requirement — but for secular reasons and not religious ones.

The appeals court was unpersuaded that the exceptions the state has so far allowed, which include letting some schools give preferences to low-income families or children with disabilities, are parallel to what the church has requested.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Google Will Turn Off Search for Schools That Reject A.I.
item.description:
Google announced Tuesday that early next year it would turn off artificial intelligence tools in its popular software for K-12 students, unless school administrators explicitly choose to make such tools available.

Executives at the tech giant said they wanted to be responsive to educators and parents who have asked for more control in how children interact with A.I.

But there is a catch: Schools that choose to restrict A.I. entirely will also lose access to Google search.

A.I. features are now a standard part of Google’s commercially available search engine. “Search and A.I. are deeply integrated,” said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. If a school has banned A.I., he added, students “will not have access to search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.”

Google is by far the dominant technology player in K-12 classrooms. Google’s suite of education apps — including Gmail, Docs and an assignment platform called Classroom — is ubiquitous. Google Chromebooks, low-cost laptops, are the most widely issued student devices in U.S. schools. And Google is synonymous with internet search, a crucial tool for students across the globe.

The company’s new strategy underscores Google’s powerful role in American education. If school leaders want continued student access to search within the company’s ecosystem, they will be forced to embrace Google’s A.I.

Lina Khan, a former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, said in a statement that Google was using its “search monopoly to coerce schools” into adopting its A.I. She added that multiple courts had found the tech giant liable for violating antitrust laws.

“This latest move shows it remains unchastened,” Ms. Khan said of Google’s new A.I. changes for schools. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools,” she added, “Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

In recent months, Google has been promoting its Gemini chatbot as a valuable educational tool, saying it can aid teachers in planning lessons and serve as a personalized tutor for students. A new student feature within Gemini, Guided Learning, is supposed to make it harder for students to use A.I. to cheat.

“We’re evolving our approach,” said Mr. Phillips. He promised tools that would “support the productive struggle” of learning and tamp down on students turning to A.I. for easy answers.

In August, Google turned on A.I. features as the default option inside its Classroom app for K-12 schools that had allowed students separate access to the company’s Gemini chatbot. The move upset some school leaders, who felt schools should be able to decide how and when students used Google’s A.I.

Google’s August change will now be reversed.

Parent activists have been pushing back against the use of A.I. in schools, and against screen time more generally. While A.I. chatbots can be useful tools for research and coding, they can also easily be used to cheat on school assignments and can provide false information. Research shows chatbots can also hinder critical thinking and ensnare adolescents in emotional dependency.

Last week, New York State passed a chatbot safety law that would prohibit companies from providing a variety of A.I. features for minors. And in September, the nation’s two largest school districts, in New York City and Los Angeles — both Google clients — broadly restricted student access to generative artificial intelligence on school devices.

In response to Google’s Tuesday announcement, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City wrote on social media, “No corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children. Our public schools exist to serve students, not to grow the profit margin of Big Tech.”

Officials in the Los Angeles Unified School District have said that they were hoping students would be able to conduct Google searches with A.I. overviews turned off. The overviews are A.I.-generated summaries that appear at the top of searches. They can dissuade students from seeking out multiple sources of information.

On Monday, Google executives said that for districts that do allow A.I., there will be two options for search inside school-issued accounts, beginning in early 2027. One option will be search with A.I. overviews and A.I. chats turned on, similar to the current consumer experience. The other will be search using Guided Learning, the student feature within Google’s Gemini chatbot.

Guided Learning is intended to guide students through a topic step-by-step without providing them with answers that could short-circuit learning. It is supposed to offer an experience modeled on one-to-one tutoring.

The consumer version of Guided Learning is already available within Gemini, and can enable cheating. In a reporter’s test, it produced a detailed essay in response to an Advanced Placement history prompt.

There are greater restrictions in the school version that is currently being piloted, according to Brit Mennuti, product lead for Google Classroom. She said teachers would be able to review students’ chatbot transcripts, among other capabilities.

Richard Culatta, the chief executive of ISTE+ASCD, a nonprofit group promoting “meaningful” school technology use, applauded Google’s plan to turn off its A.I. services for students by default in K-12 schools.

Tech companies, he added, should also enable schools to turn off AI features within search engines. “Our position is that schools should be able to have search that does not have A.I.-generated results in it for students,” Mr. Culatta said. (Mr. Culatta’s group has received funding from Google and other tech companies.)

Kelly Clancy is a New York City public school parent and leader in groups calling for an A.I. moratorium in schools.

She said her seventh-grade son used Google search daily to complete assignments, such as a recent earth science project that required him to learn about lab safety.

“We have to go back to the drawing board on how we are teaching kids to research,” she said, suggesting that students could use alternatives such as physical libraries or competing search engines that allow more control over A.I.

Morgan Polikoff, an education professor at the University of Southern California, said Google’s decision could further energize the anti-tech movement percolating among parents and educators.

“This is a particularly clear example of the tech industry going out of its way to force A.I. on us all — even if we have said we don’t want it,” he said.

item.title: When Children Are Charged With Crimes
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “In Texas, Minor Misdeeds Can Get a Young Student Arrested” (news article, Oct. 21):

Aggressive police actions like those described in Texas schools — handcuffing, restraining and detaining young children, whose behavior is reflective of their immaturity and sometimes their special needs — can occur only when states fail to set a rational minimum age for prosecution in juvenile court.

When schools are unable to refer children to court or delegate discipline to law enforcement, they develop more appropriate, more effective and safer responses to student misbehavior.

Yet contrary to international human rights standards and common sense, nearly half of all states have no minimum jurisdictional age, and 15 others, including Texas, permit the prosecution of children as young as 10. Even in those states where prosecution of younger children is generally prohibited, furthermore, carve-outs often exist for more serious offenses.

Such criminalization of childhood runs counter to developmental science, drives the school-to-prison pipeline, disrupts families, undermines public safety and needlessly traumatizes the young.

It is for these reasons that organizations as diverse as the Society for Adolescent Mental Health and Medicine, Youth Correctional Leaders for Justice and the American Bar Association have called on states to pass laws setting a minimum age of 14, while a host of others, including the American Academy of Pediatrics, recommend a minimum age of at least 12.

Texas would do well to heed those calls.

Laura CohenNewarkThe writer is a professor at Rutgers Law School and the director of the Rutgers Criminal and Youth Justice Clinic.

To the Editor:

A 10-year-old accused of misbehaving in school should never face the possibility of arrest. Yet Texas schools are increasingly sending children as young as 10 into the juvenile legal system for nonviolent actions like vaping or “lashing out.” This is what happens when schools turn to the police and use punitive measures instead of supporting students.

A police presence doesn’t necessarily make schools safer; it risks criminalizing children, disproportionately harming Black, brown and Native youth, L.G.B.T.Q. students and students with disabilities. Several states have taken a different approach and experienced improved outcomes.

In California, for example, state law generally prohibits prosecuting children younger than 12 and requires counties to develop alternatives. Restorative justice and teacher training programs have effectively addressed students’ needs without police involvement.

Children deserve schools that help them learn and grow. Displaying common childhood behaviors at school should never result in criminal charges.

Darya LarizadehOakland, Calif.The writer is the director of California Policy and Capacity Building, Youth Justice at the National Center for Youth Law.

To the Editor:

Re “Shadows, Mirrors and ‘You Can See Everything,’” by Eve Sneider (Opinion guest essay, Oct. 28):

In her essay about the documentary “You Can See Everything,” Ms. Sneider suggests that “there’s artifice present in any work of nonfiction,” as if that is a problem only for authors or filmmakers trying to present a true story. She refers to the work of the author Janet Malcolm to support her claim.

The main point of her essay, it seems, is that art gets in the way of truth. But the problem is broader. Each of us carries around a set of beliefs that warp and shape our experience. Philosophers, most notably W.V. Quine, have called this our “web of belief.”

This web shapes all of our experience. It is not the problem of not being able to see everything, as the essay suggests, but that we are human beings with experiences that help us to understand what we are currently experiencing. Art may be what shapes the artist’s product, but life is what shapes everyone’s accounts of experiences.

So what happens to truth? Truth is what we continue to hold on to as we communicate with others and add to our webs.

Sharon SchwarzeWayne, Pa.The writer is a professor emerita of philosophy at Cabrini University.
